title: Words in Context
lead: Some Reading and Writing questions give you a short text with a blank and ask: “Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?” They are among the most common questions on the test. They reward careful reading at least as much as a large vocabulary.

parts.title: Part 1 · What “precise” means
parts.html:
A precise word is the one that says exactly what the sentence needs. It fits the grammar, and it also supports the point the text is making.

That second half is where most mistakes happen. A choice can sound fine and look impressive and still be wrong, because it says something the text does not say. So the job is to understand the text first and choose the word second.

Two things settle almost every question: context and connotation.

parts.title: Part 2 · Context: the text says it twice
parts.html:
Context is the situation the word has to fit, and you only get it by reading the whole text closely.

The test cannot ask for a word without telling you what it should mean, so the meaning of the blank appears a second time somewhere else in the text. Most of these texts follow one pattern: a statement, then the same idea restated. Your task is to find the part of the restatement that lines up with the blank.

In recommending Bao Phi’s collection Sông I Sing, a librarian noted that pieces by the spoken-word poet don’t lose their ______ nature when printed: the language has the same pleasant musical quality on the page as it does when performed by Phi. A) jarring   B) scholarly   C) melodic   D) personal

Put the two halves side by side:

  • The poems keep their ______ nature when printed.
  • The poems have the same pleasant musical quality on the page.

The blank sits in the same place as “pleasant musical quality”, so the answer is the choice closest to “pleasant and musical”: melodic, choice C.

parts.title: Part 3 · Connotation: the feeling of a word
parts.html:
Connotation is what a word suggests beyond its dictionary meaning, most often whether it feels positive or negative. Two words can describe the same fact and still not be interchangeable.

Same basic meaningPositiveNegative
Careful with moneythriftystingy
Sure of oneselfconfidentarrogant
A sign of what is comingpromisingominous

If you are stuck, read the sentence for its mood. A team’s play “suggests a bright future” needs the positive word (promising). Clouds that “suggest a storm is coming” need the negative one (ominous). A sentence that praises needs a word that praises.

parts.title: Part 4 · The three-step method
parts.html:
1. Say the text in your own words. Read it closely; do not skim. If it is dense, reduce each idea to a short bullet in your head. Expect the pattern from Part 2: a claim, then the claim again in other words.
  2. Find the key word, phrase or idea. Everything you need is in the text. There is usually one word or phrase that means almost the same as the correct answer. Once you have found that clue, the rest is quick.
  3. Pick the choice that matches. A choice is wrong if it changes the meaning of the text or brings in an idea or attitude that was not there. Only one choice repeats and strengthens what the text already says.

parts.title: Part 5 · Tips that save points
parts.html:
TipHow to use it
Mark the blank + or −Decide whether the text is positive, negative or neutral about the thing in the blank, then cross out every choice with the wrong charge.
Reuse the textLook for a word or phrase in the text that could go in the blank as it is, then find its synonym in the choices. When the blank is a noun, check what follows “this” or “these” later in the text (“these artifacts”, “this tragedy”): that noun is often the synonym. Less often the clue is an opposite, and you need an antonym.
ColonsA colon announces an explanation or an example. If the blank comes before a colon, the clue is usually right after it.
TransitionsWords like similarly, however, previously, for instance, therefore tell you how two ideas relate. Contrast words (however, regardless, although) are especially common in these questions, and they flip the meaning you need. Class 23 covers transitions in full.
Unknown wordsDo not choose a word because you have never seen it, and do not reject a word you know because it “seems too easy”. First eliminate what you can among the words you know. Choose an unknown word only if every known word is out.
RootsA word you have never seen may share a root with one you know. If you know “negative”, you can guess that “negate” has a related meaning. Part 7 lists the most useful roots.

Five habits that help on every Reading and Writing question:

  • Skip a question stem that never changes. For blank questions the stem is always the same sentence. Read the text, not the stem.
  • Strip the details. Titles, researchers’ names and dates rarely matter. Reduce the text to who did what and what was found.
  • Do not stall on a hard word in the text. Guess its rough meaning from the sentence and keep going. The overall point usually makes it clear.
  • Shorten the jargon. Read Dermochelys coriacea as “D.C.” You will never be asked to define a technical term.
  • Eliminate, then guess. Cross out what you know is wrong and choose from what is left. A wrong answer costs nothing.

parts.title: Part 6 · Two worked examples
parts.html:
In 1929 the Atlantic Monthly published several articles based on newly discovered letters allegedly exchanged between President Abraham Lincoln and a woman named Ann Rutledge. Historians were unable to ______ the authenticity of the letters, however, and quickly dismissed them as a hoax. A) validate   B) interpret   C) relate   D) accommodate

Use the transition. “However” sets the second sentence against the first: the letters were published as real, but historians called them a hoax. With “unable to” in front of the blank, the historians could not confirm that the letters were real. The choice that means confirm is validate, choice A.

Some researchers believe that the genes that enable groundhogs and certain other mammals to hibernate through the winter by slowing their breathing and heart rates and lowering their body temperature may be ______ in humans: present yet having essentially no effect on our bodily processes. A) decisive   B) lacking   C) variable   D) dormant

Use the colon and reuse the text. What follows the colon is the definition of the blank: “present yet having essentially no effect”. The word for something that is there but inactive is dormant, choice D. “Lacking” fails because the text says the genes are present.

parts.title: Part 7 · Word parts as a backup tool
parts.html:
Use word parts when a choice is unfamiliar, and always finish with the plug-it-into-the-sentence test. A word part gives the general direction of a meaning; only the context gives the exact one.

PrefixSignalsExample
un-, in-, im-, il-, dis-, non-not, oppositeunyielding, impartial, illegible
re-again, backreinforce, retract
pre-, fore-beforeprecursor
post-afterposthumous
sub-, super-, hyper-under, above, beyondsubordinate
inter-, trans-between, acrossinterdependent, transmit
mono-, bi-, poly-one, two, manymonotony
SuffixMakesExample
-tion, -ment, -ness, -itynounspreservation, assessment, eagerness, plausibility
-ify, -ize, -ateverbsclarify, emphasize
-ous, -ful, -ive, -able, -ishadjectivesprecarious, inventive, manageable
-lyusually adverbscautiously (but: friendly, likely are adjectives)
RootMeaningExample
ben- / mal-good / badbeneficial, malevolent
dictsay, tellpredict, contradict
spectlookinspect, retrospect, circumspect (cautious)
credbelievecredible, credulous (too ready to believe)
loqu / locspeakeloquent, loquacious (talkative)
chrontimechronological, anachronistic
anthrophumananthropology, misanthrope
ambi- / amphi-both, aroundambivalent (pulled both ways)

Example. A choice is “loquacious” and the clue says the scientist “rarely used more words than necessary”. The root loqu (speak) tells you the word is about talking, so it is worth testing. Plug it in: does “talkative” fit a scientist who rarely speaks? No, it reverses the idea, so reject it. The root gets you to the right neighbourhood; the clue makes the decision.

Common mistake. Never let a word part decide on its own. “Inflammable” looks like “not flammable” but means flammable. “Nonplussed” looks like calm but means confused. And not every look-alike shares a root: “laconic” (using few words) comes from Laconia, not from loqu.

Word-form questions. When the choices are forms of one word (differ, different, difference, differently), decide what the blank must be grammatically: a thing, an action, or a description. Then the suffix decides.

parts.title: Part 8 · Signal words and the charge of the blank
parts.html:
The clue to a blank is rarely far away, and a small linking word usually tells you how the clue relates to it. These words come in three families.

FamilyExamplesWhat the blank must do
Continuersand, also, as well as, moreover, likewise, similarly, not only … but alsoGo in the same direction as the idea it is joined to
Cause and explanationbecause, since, therefore, thus, as a result; also a colon or a dashFit as the reason or the result of what is next to it
Contradictorsbut, however, although, despite, whereas, while, unlike, neverthelessGo in the opposite direction from the idea it is set against
Contradictor. On the map, the mountain road looks ______. In fact, it is full of sharp turns that slow even experienced drivers. “In fact” sets the reality against the map → the blank is the opposite of “full of sharp turns” → straight, direct

Two phrases that are easy to misread. “For all” at the start of a clause means despite: “For all its fame, the painting is small.” “All but” means almost: “The species has all but disappeared” means it has nearly disappeared, not that everything else has.

A positive idea can need a negative word. Marking the blank + or − (Part 5) is about the word, not the sentence. A negating word such as less, not, hardly or far from in front of the blank flips the charge.

Example. Early reviews called the film a failure. Later critics were far less ______, however, and several now rank it among the director's best. A) enthusiastic
B) dismissive
C) curious
D) familiar The later critics liked the film, so the idea is positive. But the blank follows “far less”. Less of something good would be negative, which is the wrong direction, so the word itself must be negative: they were less dismissive. B. A student who marks the sentence + and stops there picks A.

Matching pairs. When a sentence gives two descriptions and then explains both, the explanations line up with the descriptions in order.

The new sorting machine has been praised as both fast and ______: it handles a full crate in under a minute and almost never puts an item in the wrong bin. “under a minute” ↔ fast
“almost never … the wrong bin” ↔ the blank → accurate, precise

parts.title: Part 9 · Second meanings
parts.html:
A second, less common question asks: “As used in the text, what does the word ______ most nearly mean?” The word is nearly always an ordinary one used in a less ordinary sense. Its everyday meaning is usually among the choices, and it is usually wrong.

  1. Cover the word and read the sentence around it.
  2. Put in your own word.
  3. Choose the match. Go back to the everyday meaning only if nothing else fits.
WordEveryday meaningSecond meaningIn a sentence
checkto look at, to verifyto slow or stopHigh prices checked demand.
coina piece of moneyto invent (a word or phrase)She coined the term in 1962.
sounda noisesolid, reliablea sound argument
novela long storynew, originala novel approach
wantto wish fora lackfor want of evidence
championa winnerto support publiclyHe championed the reform.
harbora portto hold (a feeling or belief)to harbor doubts
gravea burial placeseriousa grave error
reservationsbookingsdoubtsShe had reservations about the plan.
tablefurnitureto set aside for laterThe committee tabled the proposal.

The choices are always the same part of speech. If three choices are clearly adjectives and the fourth is a word you know as a noun, that fourth word is being used as an adjective too, in a second meaning. Do not cross it out because it “does not fit”. This also happens in ordinary blank questions.

Words that look negative and are not. A prefix such as in- or un- usually signals “not”, but not always.

WordMeaning
invaluableextremely valuable
ingeniousvery clever
innocuousharmless
unassumingmodest
unqualified (success, support)complete, without limits
critic, criticismsomeone who judges a work; the judgment may be praise

Words that describe arguments. These appear in passages and, more often, in answer choices on every kind of reading question. Add them to the daily routine first.

IdeaWords
Put forward a claimpropose, posit, hypothesize, contend
Strengthen a claimsupport, bolster, corroborate, substantiate
Weaken or reject a claimchallenge, undermine, refute, dispute
Doubtskepticism, reservations, ambivalence (mixed feelings)
A small amount / a large amountscarcity, dearth, paucity / abundance, wealth, profusion
Built in from the startinherent, innate, intrinsic

Tip. Judge a word by what it means, not by how it sounds in the sentence. A correct choice can sound odd because you have not met that use of the word before. If its meaning is what the text needs, it is the answer.

parts.title: Part 10 · How wrong answers are built
parts.html:
This part applies to every reading question in the course. The information you need is always in the text, but the answer itself is usually not: correct choices restate the text's idea in different, often more general, words. A choice that repeats a phrase from the text word for word deserves more suspicion, not less.

Every wrong choice is wrong for a reason you can name.

TypeWhat it looks like
Off topicAbout something the text does not discuss
Too broadThe text describes one scientist or one species; the choice says “scientists” or “animals”
Too extremealways, never, completely, proves where the text says often, may, suggests
Half rightMostly accurate, with one word that makes it false
Could be trueReasonable, but the text does not say it
True, but not the answerAccurate about the text, but about a different part from the one the question asks about
True in the real worldA fact you know from outside that the text never states

When two choices are left, the wrong one is almost always “half right” or “could be true”.

  • Read the question before the text. It tells you what to look for and what you can skim.
  • Answer in your own words first. A few rough words are enough. Choices are written to make wrong answers sound right, so arrive with an idea of your own.
  • Down to two? Go back to the text. Do not stare at the choices. Pick one specific word in each choice and check whether the text supports it.
  • Every word in a choice counts. One wrong word makes the whole choice wrong. The more a choice says, the more there is that can be wrong.
  • Confusing is not the same as wrong. Never cross out a choice because you do not understand it. Cross out only what you can show is wrong.
  • Fit the answer to the text, not the text to the answer. If a choice works only when you read the text in a special way, it is not the answer.
  • Never read half a sentence. The first half can reverse the second: “Although the trial was small, it showed…”
